## Description

A world reclaimed by nature. The Institute's buildings still stand, but they are crumbling, overgrown with vines and moss. The sky is real — vast, changing, sometimes grey, sometimes blindingly blue. The air smells of earth and rain and decay. It is beautiful and terrifying in equal measure.

## History

When the Institute sealed itself, the outside world was dying. But four hundred years is a long time. The planet healed. The humans who couldn't enter the Institute perished, but the world they left behind grew green and wild. The children who emerge from The I will find a world that doesn't need them — one that has moved on.

## Livelihood

Hunting, foraging, farming — the basics of survival. Nothing is provided. The children must learn to find food, build shelter, make fire. The skills they need are not the ones the Institute taught them. The world demands competence, not compliance.

## Power

There is no Administrator here. Nature is the only authority — weather, terrain, predators, disease. The strong survive. The adaptable survive. The children will learn a new hierarchy: not obedience, but understanding. The world teaches through consequence, not instruction.

## Rituals

The changing of the seasons marks time. The first rain after drought. The hunt. The harvest. The burial. These are not celebrations — they are acknowledgments. The world has rhythms, and survival depends on learning them.

## Values

What the real world holds sacred: life. Not human life specifically, but the continuation of living systems. Nature is not cruel — it is honest. It does not punish or reward. It simply is. The children who learn this will survive. Those who don't will join the soil.

## Conflict

The real world is not hostile, but it is indifferent. It will not welcome the children, nor will it reject them. They will have to learn to live in a world that was never designed for them — a world where nothing appears when hunger strikes, where the light is not always correct, where survival is not guaranteed.
